arXiv:1705.01383v1 [math.OC] 03 May 2017

Internal control of systems of semilinear coupled 1-D wave equations

Christophe ZHANG
Abstract

We prove the internal controllability of some systems of two coupled wave equations in one space dimension, with one control, under certain conditions on the coupling. To do this we apply the “fictitious control method” in two cases: general systems with a “non-degenerate” coupling, and a particular case where the coupling is “degenerate”, namely a cubic coupling.

In the latter case, our proof requires to find nontrivial trajectories of the control system that go from 0\displaystyle 0 to 0\displaystyle 0. We build these trajectories by adapting (in 1\displaystyle 1 space dimension) a construction developed by Jean-Michel Coron, Sergio Guerrero and Lionel Rosier for the study of coupled parabolic systems.

Keywords. Wave equations, coupled systems, exact internal controllability, fictitious control method, algebraic solvability, return method.

1.2 Related results

Boundary controllability results for quasilinear first order hyperbolic systems, coupled or not, can be found in Tatsien Li’s book ([Li10, chapter 3]).

As for second order systems, results of global boundary and internal controllability for the semilinear wave equation are well known, and were first proven by Enrique Zuazua in [Zua93] and [Zua91]. These articles introduced the use of HUM (Hilbert Uniqueness Method) to prove controllability results for semilinear and quasilinear equations. Boundary controllability results for scalar systems with C2\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{2} regularity can be found in [Li10, chapter 5], and can be adapted to coupled systems, and for Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k} regularity.

Regarding controllability with a reduced number of controls, results for boundary and internal control of linear wave systems with a reduced number of controls have been proved by Fatiha Alabau-Boussouira ([ABL13] and [AB13]) in any space dimension, using energy methods. This was used by Fatiha Alabau Boussouira in [AB14] to prove the existence of insensitizing controls for a single wave equation, as this is linked to the controllability of linear cascade systems in one space dimension, with the same speed in both equations.

In the nonlinear case, Louis Tebou followed the same path for semilinear equations in [Teb11], where he proves the controllability of cascade systems of the form:

{□​u+f⁡(u)=h+ξ,□​v+f′​(u)​v=0,u=0,v⁡(t,0)=∂u∂n​χΓ0​on​∂Ω,\left\{\begin{aligned} \square u+f(u)&=h+\xi,\\ \square v+f^{\prime}(u)v&=0,\\ u=0,v(t,0)&=\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\chi_{\Gamma_{0}}\ \textrm{on}\ \partial\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (1.15)

where Γ0\displaystyle\Gamma_{0} is a portion of the boundary, and where f\displaystyle f is subject to a growth constraint to have global well-posedness. To prove the controllability of such systems, the author first establishes the controllability of a linear problem, using a form of HUM combined with Carleman estimates. Then, using the Schauder fixed-point theorem, he establishes the controllability of the nonlinear problem.

A similar strategy of proof appears in [CGR10] for parabolic systems with cubic coupling. In this case, as for system (1.2), the linearised system around the equilibrium (0,0,0)\displaystyle(0,0,0) is not controllable. A classical tool to handle this problem in finite dimension is the use of iterated Lie brackets, see for example [Isi95, chapter 2], [NvdS90, chapter 3], and [Cor07, chapter 3]. However, this tool does not work (see for example [Cor07, chapter 5]) for many partial differential equations, including our control system (1.2). In that case, a method to handle this situation is the return method. It consists in looking for trajectories going from 0\displaystyle 0 to 0\displaystyle 0 and such that the linearised system around them is controllable (return trajectories). This method has been introduced in [Cor92] for the stabilisation of driftless control systems and in [Cor96] and in [Cor93] for the controllability of the Euler equations of incompressible fluids. Following this method, in [CGR10] the authors build return trajectories, using the structure of the coupling. Then, using Carleman estimates, they prove the controllability of a family of related parabolic linear systems close to the return trajectory, from which they deduce null-controllability using Kakutani’s fixed-point theorem.

In other cases, a phenomenon of loss of derivatives can occur when working with Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k} regularities: this can be handled with an inversion theorem of the Nash-Moser type, with a stronger condition on the linearised system. This was done in the case for quasilinear first order hyperbolic systems, which have been studied in [ABCO17], using the “fictitious control method”, which we will explain in the following section. More precisely the result that has been obtained concerns systems of the form:

{ut+Λ1​(u,v)​(u,v)+f1​(u,v)=h,vt+Λ2​(u,v)​(u,v)+f2​(u,v)=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}+\Lambda_{1}(u,v)(u,v)+f_{1}(u,v)&=h,\\ v_{t}+\Lambda_{2}(u,v)(u,v)+f_{2}(u,v)&=0.\end{aligned}\right.

with

∂f2∂u​(0,0)≠0.\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(0,0)\neq 0. (1.16)

1.3 The fictitious control method

The fictitious control method was introduced in [Cor92] and [GBPGa05], and successfully used in [CL14], [ABCO17] and[CG17]. The idea is to first prove a controllability result with two controls (the fictitious controls), then reduce the number of controls, using some sort of fixed-point theorem.

In this article, we apply it to second order hyperbolic systems, which present the same problem of loss of derivatives as the systems in [ABCO17]. This loss of derivatives is handled by using Gromov’s notion of algebraic solvability, which allows for differential operators to be inverted in a special way under some condition (infinitesimal inversion) on their derivative. This yields local results around the equilibrium, but we will also work around other trajectories than the stationary trajectory at the equilibrium, in the spirit of the return method, paying close attention to the regularities involved. Indeed, condition (1.10) from Theorem 1.1 is identical to condition (1.16), and is crucial to solving the system algebraically (see Proposition 2.2). If, as in Theorem 1.2, it is not satisfied, then, following the spirit of the return method, one can build trajectories of the system along which such a condition is verified, at least on some appropriate spatial domain.

Remark 1.1.

In both cases, conditions (1.10) and (1.16) appear as a sufficient condition on the coupling for internal controllability with a reduced number of controls. However there is no indication (except in trivial cases like the linearised system above) that this sort of condition is necessary.

We can thus sum up our strategy of proof in three steps:

  1. 1.

    When necessary, find smooth trajectories around which Theorem 2.1 can be used.

  2. 2.

    Prove a local controllability result with two controls (fictitious controls) around the return trajectory, using classical boundary control results.

  3. 3.

    Use Theorem 2.1 to reduce the number of controls to one.

This article is organised as follows: in section 2, we illustrate Gromov’s ideas on a linear example, and then prove Theorem 1.1, which is a case where we do not need to find return trajectories. This will allow us to present how Gromov’s ideas can be applied in a nonlinear setting. In section 3 we prove Theorem 1.2. In this case we need to find return trajectories, and the application of Theorem 2.1 around those trajectories will require a more detailed knowledge of the supports of the return trajectory. Finally section 4 is devoted to possible improvements and further questions on this topic.

2 The non-degenerate case

As mentioned in section 1.3, we build on the method presented in [ABCO17]. One of the main ingredients of this method is the theory of differential operators, and the notion of algebraic solvability, which we briefly present in the subsection below. The use of algebraic solvability in the study of control systems first appears in [Cor92], where it was used to prove the stabilisability of finite dimensional systems without drift with time-varying feedbacks. It was first used in the context of partial differential equations in [CL14] for the control of the Navier-Stokes equation.

But first let us give an informal explanation of our method in the case of a linear system: first we have to rewrite the control problem using differential operators. We note 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} the operator associated with the equation of our control problem. Then, the control problem, given initial and final conditions, consists in finding (u,v)\displaystyle(u,v) with those initial and final conditions, and a control h\displaystyle h such that

𝒟⁡(u,v,h)=0.\mathscr{D}(u,v,h)=0.

This corresponds to an inversion problem, but with a twist: one has to find an inverse image with the right initial and final conditions. Now, using the solutions to forward- and backward-evolving Cauchy problems corresponding to the initial and final conditions, one can build functions (u,v)\displaystyle(u,v) with the right initial and final conditions. The nonlinear version of this is done at the beginning of subsection 2.2. In general, one can do this so that for some η>0\displaystyle\eta>0,

(h1,h2):=𝒟⁡(u,v,0)=0,∀t∉[η,T−η].(h_{1},h_{2}):=\mathscr{D}(u,v,0)=0,\forall t\notin[\eta,T-\eta].

Now suppose 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} is invertible. We can make the following computation, the nonlinear version of which is made in subsection 2.2:

𝒟⁡((u,v,0)+𝒟−1​(−h1,−h2))=(h1,h2)−(h1,h2)=0.\mathscr{D}\left((u,v,0)+\mathscr{D}^{-1}(-h_{1},-h_{2})\right)=(h_{1},h_{2})-(h_{1},h_{2})=0.

This seems to yield a solution to the control problem, however we still need to check that the “corrective term” does not change the initial and final conditions. This is where Gromov’s notion of algebraic solvability comes into play: the right property for 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} is not to be invertible, but to be algebraically solvable. That is, that the inverse can also be written as a differential operator:

𝒟−1​(−h1,−h2)=∑rar​∂r(−h1)+∑rbr​∂r(−h2)\mathscr{D}^{-1}(-h_{1},-h_{2})=\sum_{r}a_{r}\partial_{r}(-h_{1})+\sum_{r}b_{r}\partial_{r}(-h_{2})

for some functions ar,br\displaystyle a_{r},b_{r}. With this additional property, one can see that, because −h1,−h2\displaystyle-h_{1},-h_{2} vanish for t∉[η,T−η]\displaystyle t\notin[\eta,T-\eta],

𝒟−1​(−h1,−h2)=0,∀t∉[η,T−η].\mathscr{D}^{-1}(-h_{1},-h_{2})=0,\forall t\notin[\eta,T-\eta].

Hence, (u,v,0)+𝒟−1​(−h1,−h2)\displaystyle(u,v,0)+\mathscr{D}^{-1}(-h_{1},-h_{2}) still has the right initial and final conditions.

2.1 Differential relations and Gromov’s theorem

In this section we sum up some basic notions regarding differential operators, and Gromov’s local inversion theorem for differential operators. More details can be found in [Gro86].

In what follows, 𝒬\displaystyle\mathcal{Q} is the closure of a non-empty open bounded smooth subset of ℝ2\displaystyle\mathbb{R}^{2}, and p,q,r∈ℕ∗\displaystyle p,q,r\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}. We note nr,p:=2+p​ card​{(α1,α2)∈ℕ2|α1+α2≤r}\displaystyle n_{r,p}:=2+p\textup{ card}\{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\ |\ \alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\leq r\}. Recall the definition of the r\displaystyle r-jet of a function z∈Cr​(𝒬)p\displaystyle z\in\mathit{C}^{r}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}:

Jr​z​(t,x)=((t,x),z⁡(t,x),⋯,∂|α|z∂tα1​∂xα2,⋯,∂rz∂tα1​∂xα2)∈ℝnr,p,∀(t,x)∈𝒬.J^{r}z(t,x)=\left((t,x),z(t,x),\cdots,\frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}z}{\partial t^{\alpha_{1}}\partial x^{\alpha_{2}}},\cdots,\frac{\partial^{r}z}{\partial t^{\alpha_{1}}\partial x^{\alpha_{2}}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{r,p}},\ \forall(t,x)\in\mathcal{Q}.
Definition 2.1.

A map 𝒟:Cr​(𝒬)p→C0​(𝒬)q\displaystyle\mathscr{D}:\mathit{C}^{r}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}\rightarrow\mathit{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Q})^{q} is a C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} nonlinear differential operator of order r\displaystyle r if there exists F∈C∞​(ℝnr,p,ℝq)\displaystyle F\in\mathit{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n_{r,p}},\mathbb{R}^{q}) such that

𝒟⁡(z)=F⁡(Jr​z),∀z∈Cr​(𝒬)p.\mathscr{D}(z)=F(J^{r}z),\ \forall z\in\mathit{C}^{r}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}.

This clearly implies that 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} is C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} (with the usual Cr,C0\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{r},\mathit{C}^{0} topologies), and we denote by

ℒz:Cr​(𝒬)p→C0​(𝒬)q\mathscr{L}_{z}:\mathit{C}^{r}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}\rightarrow\mathit{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Q})^{q}

its Fréchet differential at z∈Cr​(𝒬)p\displaystyle z\in\mathit{C}^{r}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}.

We now define some sort of manifold, over which we can invert these operators:

Definition 2.2.

A subset 𝒜\displaystyle\mathcal{A} of Cd​(𝒬)p\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{d}(\mathcal{Q})^{p} is a differential relation of order d∈ℕ\displaystyle d\in\mathbb{N} if there exists ℛ⊂ℝnd,p\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{d,p}} such that

𝒜={z∈Cd(𝒬)p|∀(t,x)∈𝒬,Jdz(t,x)∈ℛ}.\mathcal{A}=\{z\in\mathit{C}^{d}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}\ |\ \forall(t,x)\in\mathcal{Q},J^{d}z(t,x)\in\mathcal{R}\}.

It is said to be open if ℛ\displaystyle\mathcal{R} is an open subset of ℝnd,p\displaystyle\mathbb{R}^{n_{d,p}}. For k∈ℕ\displaystyle k\in\mathbb{N}, we note

𝒜k:=𝒜∩Ck​(𝒬)p\mathcal{A}^{k}:=\mathcal{A}\cap\mathit{C}^{k}(\mathcal{Q})^{p}

For classical local inversion theorems, one needs the differential at one point to be invertible. Here the requirement is somewhat stronger: we need the differential at any point to be invertible, with the extra property that the inverse of each differential is also a linear differential operator.

Definition 2.3.

Let 𝒜⊂Cd​(𝒬)p\displaystyle\mathcal{A}\subset\mathit{C}^{d}(\mathcal{Q})^{p} be a differential relation of order d\displaystyle d, and let 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} be a differential operator of order r\displaystyle r. We say that 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} admits an infinitesimal inversion of order s∈ℕ\displaystyle s\in\mathbb{N} over 𝒜\displaystyle\mathcal{A} if there exists a family of linear differential operators of order s\displaystyle s

z∈𝒜,ℳz:Cs​(𝒬)q→C0​(𝒬)p,z\in\mathcal{A},\mathscr{M}_{z}:\mathit{C}^{s}(\mathcal{Q})^{q}\rightarrow\mathit{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Q})^{p},

such that:

  1. 1.

    For every g∈Cs​(𝒬)q\displaystyle g\in\mathit{C}^{s}(\mathcal{Q})^{q}, z↦ℳz​(g)\displaystyle z\mapsto\mathscr{M}_{z}(g) is a differential operator of order d (possibly nonlinear) and it is a C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty}-differential operator in (z,g)\displaystyle(z,g).

  2. 2.

    (Algebraic solvability) For every z∈𝒜d+r\displaystyle z\in\mathcal{A}^{d+r},

    ℒz∘ℳz=IdCr+s​(𝒬).\mathscr{L}_{z}\circ\mathscr{M}_{z}=\textrm{Id}_{\mathit{C}^{r+s}(\mathcal{Q})}.

We can now state Gromov’s inversion theorem (see [Gro86, Section 2.3.2, main theorem]):

Theorem 2.1 (Gromov).

Let 𝒜⊂Cd​(𝒬)p\displaystyle\mathcal{A}\subset\mathit{C}^{d}(\mathcal{Q})^{p} be a non-empty open differential relation of order d\displaystyle d, and let 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} be a differential operator of order r\displaystyle r. Assume that 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} admits an infinitesimal inversion of order s\displaystyle s over 𝒜\displaystyle\mathcal{A}. Let

σ0>max⁡(d,2​r+s),\sigma_{0}>\max(d,2r+s), (2.1)
ν∈(0,∞).\nu\in(0,\infty). (2.2)

Then, there exists a family of sets ℬz⊂Cσ0+s​(𝒬)q\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{z}\subset\mathit{C}^{\sigma_{0}+s}(\mathcal{Q})^{q} and a family of operators 𝒟z−1:ℬz→𝒜\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{z}^{-1}:\mathcal{B}_{z}\rightarrow\mathcal{A} where z∈𝒜σ0+r+s\displaystyle z\in\mathcal{A}^{\sigma_{0}+r+s}, such that:

    ℬ:=⋃z∈𝒜σ0+r+s{z}×ℬz\mathcal{B}:=\bigcup_{z\in\mathcal{A}^{\sigma_{0}+r+s}}\{z\}\times\mathcal{B}_{z}

  2. 2.

    (Inversion property)

    𝒟⁡(𝒟z−1​(g))=𝒟⁡(z)+g,∀(z,g)∈ℬ.\mathscr{D}\left(\mathscr{D}_{z}^{-1}(g)\right)=\mathscr{D}(z)+g,\ \forall(z,g)\in\mathcal{B}. (2.3)

  4. 4.

    𝒟z−1​(g)∈𝒜k,∀k<σ1.\mathscr{D}^{-1}_{z}(g)\in\mathcal{A}^{k},\quad\forall k<\sigma_{1}. (2.5)

    Moreover,

    (z,g)↦𝒟z−1​(g)∈C0​(𝒜σ0+r+s×ℬzσ1+s,𝒜k),∀k<σ1.(z,g)\mapsto\mathscr{D}^{-1}_{z}(g)\in\mathit{C}^{0}(\mathcal{A}^{\sigma_{0}+r+s}\times\mathcal{B}_{z}^{\sigma_{1}+s},\mathcal{A}^{k}),\quad\forall k<\sigma_{1}. (2.6)

    Finally, if η1>σ1\displaystyle\eta_{1}>\sigma_{1}, then (2.5) and (2.6) hold for k=σ1\displaystyle k=\sigma_{1}.

  5. 5.

    (Locality) For every (t,x)∈𝒬\displaystyle(t,x)\in\mathcal{Q}, and for every (z1,g1),(z2,g2)∈ℬ\displaystyle(z_{1},g_{1}),(z_{2},g_{2})\in\mathcal{B}, if we have

    (z1,g1)​(t~,x~)=(z2,g2)​(t~,x~),∀(t~,x~)∈B⁡((t,x),ν)∩𝒬,(z_{1},g_{1})(\tilde{t},\tilde{x})=(z_{2},g_{2})(\tilde{t},\tilde{x}),\ \forall(\tilde{t},\tilde{x})\in B((t,x),\nu)\cap\mathcal{Q},

    then,

    𝒟z1−1​(g1)​(t,x)=𝒟z2−1​(g2)​(t,x).\mathscr{D}_{z_{1}}^{-1}(g_{1})(t,x)=\mathscr{D}_{z_{2}}^{-1}(g_{2})(t,x).
Remark 2.1.

The neighbourhood property allows to relate the domains of inversion for each local inversion to each other: local inverses at two “neighbouring” points will be defined on domains that have “neighbouring” sizes. In particular that means the domains of inversions are bound to overlap. The locality property tells us that when this happens (albeit locally), the images of the local inverses agree locally. In the linear case, this corresponds to the fact that when a function vanishes on an open set, its image by any linear differential operator also vanishes on this open set (see the beginning of the section).

3 A degenerate case: cubic coupling

We now turn to system (1.2). Let us mention a few important specificities of this system. First, around the equilibrium (0,0,0)\displaystyle(0,0,0), the linearised system is obviously not controllable:

{□ν1​u=h,□ν2​v=0,u|∂Ω=0,v|∂Ω=0,\left\{\begin{aligned} \square_{\nu_{1}}u&=h,\\ \square_{\nu_{2}}v&=0,\\ u_{|\partial\Omega}&=0,\\ v_{|\partial\Omega}&=0,\end{aligned}\right. (3.1)

the control h\displaystyle h gives us no influence on the dynamics ofv\displaystyle v.

This fact can also be described as a degenerescence: system (1.2) does not satisfy condition (1.10), so the coupling can be seen as degenerate. Thus, the computations from the beginning of subsection 2.2 do not hold: we cannot work around the stationary trajectory 0\displaystyle 0, thus we need to find another trajectory around which to work. More precisely, keeping in mind Proposition 2.2, we look for a return trajectory (u¯,v¯,h¯)\displaystyle(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h}) going from 0\displaystyle 0 to 0\displaystyle 0 such that for some smooth closed set 𝒬⊂[0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}\subset[0,T]\times[a,b],we have

∀(t,x)∈𝒬,∂f2∂u​(u¯​(t,x),v¯​(t,x))=3​u¯2​(t,x)≠0.\forall(t,x)\in\mathcal{Q},\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial u}(\bar{u}(t,x),\bar{v}(t,x))=3\bar{u}^{2}(t,x)\neq 0. (3.2)

Additionnally, 𝒬\displaystyle\mathcal{Q} will have to satisfy some properties so that a result with two controls can be proved.

To find such a trajectory, we follow the same idea as in [CGR10], where return trajectories are built for coupled heat equations with a cubic coupling. The additional derivative in time simply adds terms and makes for heavier computations. However, condition (3.2) will account for additional work.

We will then prove and use a more general controllability result with two controls. After that, the application of Gromov’s theorem is rather straightforward.

3.1 A preliminary construction: elementary trajectories

In this subsection, we describe a construction of a smooth trajectory of system (1.2) that goes from 0\displaystyle 0 to 0\displaystyle 0. For now we consider condition (3.2) but without any special requirements for 𝒬\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}.

In what follows, we suppose, without loss of generality (by scaling the space variable) that ν2=1\displaystyle\nu_{2}=1.

To build trajectories that start at 0\displaystyle 0 and return there, the idea is to use the cascade structure of the equation: first we find a C∞​([−1,1]×[0,1])\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty}([-1,1]\times[0,1]) function v¯\displaystyle\bar{v} such that □​v¯\displaystyle\square\bar{v} is the third power of a C∞​([−1,1]×[0,1])\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty}([-1,1]\times[0,1]) function u¯\displaystyle\bar{u}. By setting the right conditions at the start and end times, this gives us a return trajectory. The corresponding control will then be □ν1​u¯\displaystyle\square_{\nu_{1}}\bar{u}.

Let us recall that x↦x3\displaystyle x\mapsto\sqrt[3]{x} is C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} on ℝ∗\displaystyle\mathbb{R}^{\ast}. So, by composition, the cubic root of a C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} function f\displaystyle f is C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} at all the points where f\displaystyle f is non-zero. At the points where f\displaystyle f vanishes, by Taylor’s formula, a fairly simple sufficient condition for f3\displaystyle\sqrt[3]{f} to be C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} at those points is for f\displaystyle f to vanish, along with its first and second derivatives, while its third derivative is non-zero.

Now, to find functions whose image by the wave operator is a third power of a C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} function, we consider the solutions to the corresponding stationary problem, namely functions whose Laplacian is the third power of a C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} function. The solution of this problem corresponds to the following proposition, proven (with 1/2\displaystyle 1/2 instead of 3/4\displaystyle 3/4) in [CGR10]:

Proposition 3.1 (Coron, Guerrero, Rosier).

There exist δ′,δ′′,g∈C∞​([0,1]),G∈C∞​([0,1])\displaystyle\delta^{\prime},\delta^{\prime\prime},g\in\mathit{C}^{\infty}([0,1]),G\in\mathit{C}^{\infty}([0,1]) such that

{g′′=G,g⁡(z)=1−z2​on​[0,δ′′],g(z)=e−11−z2on[1−δ′,1),G⁡(z)​(z−34)>0​ for ​z∈(0,1)∖{34},G⁡(z)=(z−34)3​on​[34−δ′′2,34+δ′′2],\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}g^{\prime\prime}=G,\\ g(z)=1-z^{2}\ \textup{on}\ [0,\delta^{\prime\prime}],\\ g(z)=e^{-\frac{1}{1-z^{2}}}\ \textup{on}\ [1-\delta^{\prime},1),\\ G(z)\left(z-\frac{3}{4}\right)>0\textup{ for }z\in(0,1)\setminus\left\{\frac{3}{4}\right\},\\ G(z)=\left(z-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3}\ \textup{on}\ \left[\frac{3}{4}-\frac{\delta^{\prime\prime}}{2},\frac{3}{4}+\frac{\delta^{\prime\prime}}{2}\right],\end{array}\right. Remark 3.2.

Most of the work in the construction above comes from the vanishing points (t,(3/4)​λ​(t))\displaystyle\displaystyle{\left(t,(3/4)\lambda(t)\right)} “in the middle of the domain”. So one could wonder, would it not be simpler to try and build a function that only vanishes, along with all its derivatives, at the points (t,λ⁡(t))\displaystyle\left(t,\lambda(t)\right)?

Let us remind that our strategy to build the return trajectory is to start from a solution to the stationary problem, and then make it evolve through time so as to stay “not too far away from it”. But the reason we have vanishing points “in the middle of the domain” has to do with that same stationary problem. More precisely, the stationary problem consists in finding functions that vanish, along with their derivatives, on the boundary of the domain. In our case this condition corresponds to

g⁡(z)=e−11−z2​on​[1−δ′,1].g(z)=e^{-\frac{1}{1-z^{2}}}\ \textrm{on}\ [1-\delta^{\prime},1]. (3.31)

We further require that the Laplacians of these functions be third powers of C∞\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{\infty} functions. In our case this condition becomes

G​(z)​(z−34)>0,G⁡(z)=(z−34)3​on​[34−δ′′2,34+δ′′2].\begin{array}[]{c}\displaystyle{G(z)\left(z-\frac{3}{4}\right)>0},\\ \displaystyle{G(z)=\left(z-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3}}\ \textrm{on}\ \left[\frac{3}{4}-\frac{\delta^{\prime\prime}}{2},\frac{3}{4}+\frac{\delta^{\prime\prime}}{2}\right].\end{array}

Now, we could instead demand that G\displaystyle G be non-negative (or non-positive). But then, by convexity arguments (or Hopf’s maximum principle), we would get

g′​(1)<0,g^{\prime}(1)<0,

Which contradicts condition (3.31). But that condition is very helpful in proving the smoothness of 𝒱13\displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\frac{1}{3}} near the boundary. Giving it up would mean setting more conditions on the gi\displaystyle g_{i} functions near the boundary, so we would have to give up condition (3.8), and then set additional conditions on the gi\displaystyle g_{i} to make sure V\displaystyle V is well defined (as λ⁡(0)=λ⁡(T)=0\displaystyle\lambda(0)=\lambda(T)=0), preserve the sign of 𝒱\displaystyle\mathcal{V} or more generally its smoothness, in particular near the boundary…Which would probably be more trouble than what we had to do at the vanishing points (t,(3/4)​λ​(t))\displaystyle\displaystyle{\left(t,(3/4)\lambda(t)\right)}.

3.2 Covering sets and return trajectories

As mentioned at the beginning of this section, we want to work on a smooth subset of [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b] where u≠0\displaystyle u\neq 0. However, to do so we need more than the elementary trajectory described above: rather, we use the elementary trajectory as a building block for our final return trajectory. Indeed, let 0<δ<min⁡((b−a)/4,T/2)\displaystyle 0<\delta<\min\left((b-a)/4,T/2\right) such that (2.8) is satisfied. The preliminary construction gives us a real number ε>0\displaystyle\varepsilon>0 (after the right rescaling of the space variable) and, for any x0∈[a+δ+ε,b−δ−ε]\displaystyle x_{0}\in[a+\delta+\varepsilon,b-\delta-\varepsilon], a trajectory (u¯,v¯,h¯)\displaystyle(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h}) such that u¯≠0\displaystyle\bar{u}\neq 0 on Λε,x0:={(t,x)||x−x0|<(3/4)​ε​λ0​(t)}\displaystyle\Lambda_{\varepsilon,x_{0}}:=\{(t,x)\ |\ |x-x_{0}|<(3/4)\varepsilon\lambda_{0}(t)\}, which contains any rectangle of the form [δ,T−δ]×[x0−ξ,x0+ξ]\displaystyle[\delta,T-\delta]\times[x_{0}-\xi,x_{0}+\xi] with ξ<(3/4)​ε\displaystyle\xi<(3/4)\varepsilon. Moreover, each of these rectangles can be fit into the interior of a smooth closed subset of Λε,x0\displaystyle\Lambda_{\varepsilon,x_{0}}.

Now there are cases (if [a,b]\displaystyle[a,b] is too long and ε\displaystyle\varepsilon - and consequently, ξ\displaystyle\xi - too small), where none of the rectangles [δ,T−δ]×[x0−ξ,x0+ξ]\displaystyle[\delta,T-\delta]\times[x_{0}-\xi,x_{0}+\xi] satisfies the Geometric Control Condition (GCC). Thus we cannot apply Proposition 2.1 with controls supported in some [δ,T−δ]×[x0−ξ,x0+ξ]\displaystyle[\delta,T-\delta]\times[x_{0}-\xi,x_{0}+\xi], as time condition (3.52) does not hold in these cases. So we need to build a return trajectory (u¯,v¯,h¯)\displaystyle(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h}) such that u¯≠0\displaystyle\bar{u}\neq 0 on a smooth closed set 𝒬\displaystyle\mathcal{Q} containing a set 𝒬δ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\delta} that satisfies the GCC.

Now there is a simple type of set that would fit our needs for 𝒬δ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\delta}: in Section 2 we worked in [δ,T−δ]×[a+δ,b+δ]\displaystyle[\delta,T-\delta]\times[a+\delta,b+\delta], but we do not need the whole rectangle in general for the GCC to be satisfied. We can in fact work with a number of much smaller rectangles, as long as they are close enough to each other:

Definition 3.1.

Let 0<δ<min⁡((b−a)/4,T/2)\displaystyle 0<\delta<\min\left((b-a)/4,T/2\right), such that (2.8) is satisfied. A δ\displaystyle\delta-covering set of [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b] for system (1.1) is a union of rectangles of the form {[δ,T−δ]×[ai,bi],1≤i≤N}\displaystyle\left\{[\delta,T-\delta]\times[a_{i},b_{i}],1\leq i\leq N\right\} for some N≥1\displaystyle N\geq 1, such that

Then,

is a smooth closed set such that 𝒬δ⊂𝒬∘\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\delta}\subset\overset{\circ}{\mathcal{Q}}, and we can define

which is supported in [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b], and satisfies (3.2).

Remark 3.3.

It is clear, by Definition 3.1, that for any 0<δ<min⁡((b−a)/4,T/2)\displaystyle 0<\delta<\min\left((b-a)/4,T/2\right) such that (2.8) is satisfied, [δ,T−δ]×[a+δ,b−δ]\displaystyle[\delta,T-\delta]\times[a+\delta,b-\delta] is a δ\displaystyle\delta-covering set of [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b]. 3.4 A general criterion for internal controllability

Let us now give a general definition, which gives the main criterion our return trajectories must fulfill to apply our method:

Definition 3.2.

A suitable return trajectory for time T>0\displaystyle T>0 is a trajectory (u¯,v¯,h¯)∈C11​([0,T]×[0,L])3\displaystyle(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h})\in\mathit{C}^{11}([0,T]\times[0,L])^{3} of system (1.1), such that

u¯​(0,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{u}(0,\cdot)=0, v¯​(0,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{v}(0,\cdot)=0,
u¯t​(0,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{u}_{t}(0,\cdot)=0, v¯t​(0,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{v}_{t}(0,\cdot)=0,
u¯​(T,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{u}(T,\cdot)=0, v¯​(T,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{v}(T,\cdot)=0,
u¯t​(T,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{u}_{t}(T,\cdot)=0, v¯t​(T,⋅)=0,\displaystyle\bar{v}_{t}(T,\cdot)=0,
supp​(u¯,v¯,h¯)⊂[0,T]×[a,b],\textup{supp}\ (\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h})\subset[0,T]\times[a,b],
𝒟⁡(u¯,v¯,h¯)=(0,0),\mathscr{D}(\bar{u},\bar{v},\bar{h})=(0,0),

and such that there exists 0<δ<min⁡(T/2,(b−a)/2)\displaystyle 0<\delta<\min\left(T/2,(b-a)/2\right) satisfying (2.8), a δ\displaystyle\delta-covering set 𝒬δ\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\delta}, a smooth closed set 𝒬\displaystyle\mathcal{Q} such that 𝒬δ⊂𝒬∘\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\delta}\subset\overset{\circ}{\mathcal{Q}} such that

∀(t,x)∈𝒬,u¯​(t,x)≠0.\forall(t,x)\in\mathcal{Q},\ \bar{u}(t,x)\neq 0.

We can now give a general statement to sum up our work on system (1.2):

Proposition 3.7.

Let 0≤a<b≤L\displaystyle 0\leq a<b\leq L, and T>0\displaystyle T>0 such that (1.9) holds. Suppose condition (1.10) does not hold. If one can find a suitable return trajectory, then system (1.1) is locally controllable in time T\displaystyle T for (C11×C10)4\displaystyle\left(\mathit{C}^{11}\times\mathit{C}^{10}\right)^{4} initial and final conditions, with C6\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{6} trajectories, and with a C6\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{6} control supported in [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b].

4 Further questions

4.1 Regularity

Our method requires somewhat specific regularities: C11\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{11} (C10\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{10} for the time-derivative) for the initial and final data. As is often the case when using a Nash-Noser scheme, these regularities are probably not optimal. However, if we require for example Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k} regularity for the control, k≥2\displaystyle k\geq 2, the initial and final data have to be at least one notch smoother. Indeed, note

w:=ut−ν1​ux,w:=u_{t}-\nu_{1}u_{x},

and consider to the following computation, where one requires the control and the trajectories to be Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k}:

dd​t​w​(t,x−ν1​t)=wt−ν1​wx=wt+ν1​wx−2​ν1​wx=h⁡(t,x−ν1​t)−2​ν1​(ut​x−ν1​ux​x)=h⁡(t,x−ν1​t)−2​ν1​dd​t​ux​(t,x−ν1​t),\begin{array}[]{rl}\frac{d}{dt}w(t,x-\nu_{1}t)&=w_{t}-\nu_{1}w_{x}\\ &=w_{t}+\nu_{1}w_{x}-2\nu_{1}w_{x}\\ &=h(t,x-\nu_{1}t)-2\nu_{1}(u_{tx}-\nu_{1}u_{xx})\\ &=h(t,x-\nu_{1}t)-2\nu_{1}\frac{d}{dt}u_{x}(t,x-\nu_{1}t),\end{array}

hence, for a fixed t>0\displaystyle t>0 and for characteristics going from {0}×[0,L]\displaystyle\{0\}\times[0,L] to {t}×[0,L]\displaystyle\{t\}\times[0,L],

∫0th⁡(s,x−ν1​s)​𝑑s=ut​(t,x−ν1​t)−u1​(x)−ν1​ux​(t,x−ν1​t)+ν1​u0′​(x)−2​ν1​(ux​(t,x−ν1​t)−u0′​(x)).\int_{0}^{t}h(s,x-\nu_{1}s)ds=u_{t}(t,x-\nu_{1}t)-u_{1}(x)-\nu_{1}u_{x}(t,x-\nu_{1}t)+\nu_{1}u_{0}^{\prime}(x)-2\nu_{1}(u_{x}(t,x-\nu_{1}t)-u_{0}^{\prime}(x)). (4.1)

Now the left-hand side of (4.1) is of class Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k}, so we need to upgrade the regularity of u0\displaystyle u_{0} to Ck+1\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k+1}, and that of u1\displaystyle u_{1}, x↦ux​(t,x)\displaystyle x\mapsto u_{x}(t,x) and x↦ut​(t,x)\displaystyle x\mapsto u_{t}(t,x) to Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k}. This shows a partial derivative loss (in the space dimension) between the trajectory and the control, and, taking t=T\displaystyle t=T, a derivative loss between the initial and final data for u\displaystyle u, and the control.

For linear cascade systems with smooth coefficients, the same procedure can be repeated on the second equation to establish similar losses of derivatives, showing that because u\displaystyle u has increased spatial regularity, the initial and final data for v\displaystyle v have to be Ck+2×Ck+1\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k+2}\times\mathit{C}^{k+1}. Note that with two controls, this would not be the case, as each control “absorbs” the loss of derivatives in each equation.

Furthermore, it would be interesting to consider other iteration schemes such as the one presented in [Cor07], section 4.2.1, where one considers the following linear system:

{□​u=f1​(0,0)+g1v​(a,b)​v+g1u​(a,0)​u+h□​v=f2​(0,0)+g2v​(0,b)​v+g2u​(a,b)​u,\left\{\begin{aligned} \square u&=f_{1}(0,0)+g_{1}^{v}(a,b)v+g_{1}^{u}(a,0)u+h\\ \square v&=f_{2}(0,0)+g_{2}^{v}(0,b)v+g_{2}^{u}(a,b)u,\end{aligned}\right. (4.2)

where, for i∈{1,2}\displaystyle i\in\{1,2\},

giu(u,v)={fi​(u,v)−fi​(0,v)ufor​u≠0∂ufi​(0,v)for​u=0.g_{i}^{u}(u,v)=\left\{\begin{aligned} \frac{f_{i}(u,v)-f_{i}(0,v)}{u}\ &\textrm{for}\ u\neq 0\\ \partial_{u}f_{i}(0,v)\ &\textrm{for}\ u=0.\end{aligned}\right.
giv(u,v)={fi​(u,v)−fi​(u,0)vfor​v≠0∂vfi​(u,0)for​v=0.g_{i}^{v}(u,v)=\left\{\begin{aligned} \frac{f_{i}(u,v)-f_{i}(u,0)}{v}\ &\textrm{for}\ v\neq 0\\ \partial_{v}f_{i}(u,0)\ &\textrm{for}\ v=0.\end{aligned}\right.

Then, by superposition one can restrict to the study of

{□​u=h□​v=g2u​(a,b)​u.\left\{\begin{aligned} \square u&=h\\ \square v&=g_{2}^{u}(a,b)u.\end{aligned}\right. (4.3)

But ultimately, this only shifts the problem of the Ck\displaystyle\mathit{C}^{k} regularity gap between data and control, although we now have a linear system instead of a semilinear one.

On the other hand, it is now well known that in some cases, results that were obtained using the Nash-Moser iteration scheme can also be obtained through more classical iteration schemes, see for example the works of Matthias Gunther ([G8̈9], [G9̈1]). It would be interesting to know if a similar do-over is possible for our result.

Finally, it would be interesting to investigate a Hk\displaystyle H^{k} version of this result, using other versions of the Nash-Moser implicit function theorem.

4.2 Other degenerate couplings

Our scheme of proof also allows to prove a controllability result for systems of the form

{□ν1​u=G(u,v)+h,G∈C∞(ℝ2),□ν2​v=u3,u|∂Ω=0,v|∂Ω=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} \square_{\nu_{1}}u&=G(u,v)+h,\ G\in\mathit{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\\ \square_{\nu_{2}}v&=u^{3},\\ u_{|\partial\Omega}&=0,\\ v_{|\partial\Omega}&=0.\end{aligned}\right. (4.4)

Indeed, this simply adds a term in the definition of h¯\displaystyle\bar{h} when we build our return trajectory. However, h¯\displaystyle\bar{h} is no longer supported in [0,T]×[a,b]\displaystyle[0,T]\times[a,b]. The other steps remain unchanged, as the additional G\displaystyle G term does not prevent the differential operator 𝒟\displaystyle\mathscr{D} from being algebraically solvable. So we get a local internal controllability result with the same time conditions, but no condition on the support of the control. Finally, if G\displaystyle G is homogeneous of degree 1\displaystyle 1, we can use the scaling argument to deduce a global result.

In addition to adding a coupling term to the first equation, we can also change the power of the coupling term in the second equation. There are two cases:

  1. 1.

    Even powers As such, our method cannot work for even powers: indeed, u2​k\displaystyle u^{2k} has nonnegative values. In particular, by the same convexity argument as in Remark 3.2, solutions to the stationary problem cannot vanish smoothly in 1\displaystyle 1. So the perturbative approach would allow us to build smooth return trajectories only if u\displaystyle u (and thus h\displaystyle h) is spatially supported in all of [0,L]\displaystyle[0,L].

    Another way of answering this question would be to switch to complex values, as is done in the appendix of [CGR10] for the quadratic case.

  2. 2.

    Odd powers Thanks to Proposition 3.7, we know that the part that requires the most work is the construction of return trajectories: say the power of the coupling is 2​k+1,k∈ℕ∗\displaystyle 2k+1,\ k\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}, in order to control all the derivatives of v\displaystyle v up to 2​k+1\displaystyle 2k+1, we would have to look for v\displaystyle v in the form

    ∑i=02​k+1fi​(t)​gi​(|x−b+a2|λ).\sum_{i=0}^{2k+1}f_{i}(t)g_{i}\left(\frac{|x-\frac{b+a}{2}|}{\lambda}\right).

    This would call for ever longer computations, and for now there is no indication that there might or might not be new difficulties with these additional terms.

4.3 Boundary controllability

In this article we have explored a method to prove internal controllability with one control. However, to our knowledge there is no result for boundary controllability with one control for semilinear systems such as (1.1). Although boundary controllability is relatively easy to establish for simple equations, or when there are the same number of controls and equations, we cannot use results on the inversion of differential operators to reduce the number of controls.
